Issued at 352 AM CDT Sun Jul 26 2026

...TODAY THROUGH MONDAY NIGHT...

Early this morning, water vapor satellite imagery and upper air 
analysis continues to show a large and strong mid/upper ridge across 
the southern/central Rockies and into the southern/central plains. 
The bottom line: this persistent pattern continues to be very 
supportive of hot conditions across the central plains. This 
afternoon will be much like yesterday with 500 mb heights and 850 mb 
temperatures above the 95th percentile supporting afternoon surface 
temperatures in the 100s across nearly the entire forecast area. 
While dewpoints will be lower than yesterday, they will likely 
remain in the mid 60s to low 70s. These conditions will support heat 
indices up to 110 across the forecast area, and it's possible heat 
indices could out perform what is currently forecast (much like 
yesterday). That being said, boundary layer mixing could be more 
intense than forecast for locations west of I-135 which would lead 
to dewpoints in the lower 60s. However, should this drier solution 
pan out, air temperatures will likely be a tad hotter than currently 
forecast, which would still lead to heat indices approaching 110 
across these locations. Regardless of the finer details, it will be 
hot (yes, even for summer), and those sensitive to heat will need to 
take the proper precautions if spending time outside this afternoon 
and early evening. Heat stress will continue even into the nighttime 
hours with lows struggling to fall below 80 degrees overnight.

The pattern is not expected to change much for Monday with the 
aforementioned strong upper anti-cyclone and very warm mid-level 
temperatures supporting hot surface air temperatures during the 
afternoon and early evening hours. Mid-range guidance continues to 
suggest that deep mixing, mostly due to breezy south-southwest 
winds, during the afternoon hours will likely lead to drier 
conditions on Monday; however, this will also lead to hotter 
afternoon highs. That being said, even if afternoon highs are around 
105, dewpoints in the low 60s won't drive heat indices much higher 
than that, so a heat advisory has been maintained (no upgrade to a 
warning) despite the forecast calling for hotter afternoon 
temperatures than yesterday and today. 

The forecast beyond Monday evening/night begins to become a little 
more uncertain as the aforementioned upper ridge begins to break 
down and shift westward, and a weak cold front slowly sags southward 
into Kansas overnight Monday into Tuesday morning. A complex of 
storms is likely to develop across the northern High Plains and 
progress eastward into northern Kansas and southern Nebraska during 
the overnight hours. Currently, rain chances are limited to north of 
I-70 early Tuesday morning given that very warm mid-level 
temperatures will likely be detrimental to the maintenance of 
convection south of I-70. With that being said, it is 2026, and the 
trend this year has been for convection to overperform model 
guidance. Therefore, trends will need to be monitored over the next 
36-48 hours.

...TUESDAY THROUGH SATURDAY...

Assuming that convection Monday night into Tuesday morning behaves 
as currently forecast, another hot day is likely on Tuesday, 
especially across southern and southeast Kansas. Lighter surface 
winds out of the east/southeast Tuesday afternoon is likely to 
prevent deep mixing of the boundary layer, thus dewpoints will 
likely a tad higher. Despite afternoon highs forecast to be slightly 
"cooler," heat indices should still exceed 105 across southern and 
southeast Kansas Tuesday afternoon and evening. With the primary 
ridge axis shifting westwards towards the Four Corners region, the 
mid-level baroclinic zone is forecast to be draped over Kansas late 
Tuesday night into early Wednesday morning. Model guidance suggest 
widely scattered showers and storms are possible along this feature 
early Wednesday morning with some activity possibly lingering across 
far eastern Kansas well into Wednesday afternoon. Assuming coverage 
and timing of potential convection ends up as currently forecast, 
the area will continue to feel the influence of the ridge out west 
with highs rising into the mid to upper 90s Wednesday afternoon. 
Beyond this point, details become a little less clear. However, in 
general, mid-range model guidance suggests a pattern supportive of 
periodic storm chances through the remainder of the week with a 
parade of shortwave troughs embedded in weak northwest flow sweeping 
over the region. Severe weather is not anticipated with this 
activity at this time, but stay tuned for updates over the coming 
days.
